identity.companyProfile: Tesla designs, manufactures, and sells battery-electric vehicles, alongside energy generation and storage products including Powerwall and Megapack. It reports two segments: Automotive and Energy Generation and Storage. The company also develops Full Self-Driving software, pursues a robotaxi network, and operates the Optimus humanoid robot program. Vehicle sales remain its main revenue source, while energy storage and software/autonomy are its fastest-growing and most speculative opportunities.

recommendation.twelveMonthView: Tesla trades at a massive premium driven almost entirely by unproven autonomy and robotics optionality, leaving it highly vulnerable to execution delays and continued automotive margin compression.
prose: SELL. Our 12-month target price is USD 230.2, implying 29.9% downside from the current price of USD 328.58.

The current share price assumes near-flawless execution across two highly speculative option pools: Autonomy and Optimus. Together, they account for nearly two-thirds of the USD 1.30 trillion enterprise value. The market multiple of 96.2x 2027E EV/EBITDA requires Tesla to convert 1.48 million FSD active users and early robotaxi operations into tens of billions of dollars of high-margin network revenue by 2030. It must also launch commercial humanoid robots at scale.

The evidence points to a large gap between current economics and what the valuation requires. FSD generates approximately USD 0.8 billion of annualized recurring revenue, with zero disclosed standalone profit. Recent progress includes a July 2026 milestone of 2.5 million paid robotaxi miles across seven U.S. metros (businessinsider.com). However, Automotive, the core profit engine, is weakening. After deliveries fell 8.6% in 2025, group EBIT margin declined from 16.8% in 2022 to 4.6% in 2025. This weakens the earnings support beneath the rising EV.

The strongest counterargument is Tesla's recent regulatory progress. Dutch RDW issued provisional EU type approval for FSD Supervised on 10 April 2026 (eleport.com), and Q2 2026 deliveries rose 25% year-over-year. These developments do not change our view. Supervised approvals and periodic delivery rebounds do not close the gap to unsupervised robotaxi leadership. Nor do they remove the competitive pressure from BYD in the hardware business.

We would change our view only if regulator-approved unsupervised autonomy expands successfully beyond limited U.S. pilots and Automotive gross margins stabilize structurally above 20%. Further delays to Cybercab SOP or China’s strict L3/L4 regulatory rollout would weaken Tesla's network ambitions and increase downside.

thesisReasons.title: Autonomy EV unsupported
thesisReasons.body: Autonomy and Robotaxi account for USD 578.5 billion, or 44.6% of group EV. This value assumes FSD subscriptions and robotaxi miles become high-margin revenue. Today, the segment generates only USD 0.8 billion of ARR and zero disclosed EBIT, leaving most of its value unsupported by current earnings.

thesisReasons.title: Automotive margin compression
thesisReasons.body: Automotive remains the main profit engine, but group EBIT margin fell from 16.8% in 2022 to 4.6% in 2025. Deliveries declined 8.6% in 2025 amid pricing pressure. The smaller margin base weakens the earnings support for the group's EV/EBITDA multiple.

thesisReasons.title: Premium market multiple
thesisReasons.body: The market values Tesla at 96.2x 2027E EV/EBITDA, well above the 70x multiple used to derive our USD 230.2 target. The premium reflects unproven Autonomy and Optimus optionality rather than disclosed earnings, supporting a lower target multiple and share price.

recommendation.thesisBreaker: A multi-year delay in unsupervised operations, combined with continued Automotive margin compression, would leave the option EV unsupported while the main profit engine shrinks.

sharePrice.context: Tesla's share price has been highly volatile over the past 36 months. Sentiment around autonomy and robotics has mattered more than near-term automotive earnings. Group EBIT margin fell from 16.8% in 2022 to 4.6% in 2025 as EV competition intensified, yet the stock retains a substantial premium. The market assumes successful Cybercab operations and future Optimus mass production. As the current price reflects near-flawless execution of these unproven options, our 12-month target of USD 230.2 applies a more realistic multiple.

deepDive: ### Why the market values it

The allocation values Autonomy as a call option on two monetization models that share a software stack and regulatory gate: robotaxi ride fees and FSD licensing. The current price requires these cash flows to support nearly half of Tesla's enterprise value by the end of the forecast period.
### Market structure and demand

Conservative estimates put the global robotaxi market at USD 45.7 billion in 2030. Goldman Sachs projects the U.S. market alone at USD 19 billion. Realistic market share requires unsupervised regulatory approval, volume production, and high utilization to cover operating costs.
### Competitive position and economic moat
- Waymo: 500,000 paid weekly rides; fleet of ~3,000–3,500; ~$15–17 revenue per ride
- Tesla: 2.5m paid miles in Q2; ~hundreds of active vehicles; no disclosed take-rate
- Baidu Apollo Go: ~1,000 vehicles (est. 2026); $0.80–1.50 per mile
### Unit economics and required scale

To support USD 578.5 billion of allocated EV at a 15× 2030 EBIT multiple, the segment needs roughly USD 38 billion of EBIT. That implies USD 95–110 billion of revenue at a 35–40 percent margin. This exceeds the entire conservative 2030 robotaxi market.
### Economics bridge and gap
Allocated EV is USD 578.5 billion, versus roughly USD 0.8 billion of FSD ARR and zero disclosed EBIT today. Closing this gap requires broad unsupervised regulatory approval and mass production.
### Milestones and evidence needed
- Next 12–24 months: expand unsupervised service beyond 7 U.S. metros
- First EU or China unsupervised permit and start of Cybercab volume production
- Disclosure of robotaxi take-rate or unit contribution margin
### Assessment
Speculative. The allocation assumes a dominant position in a market whose 2030 size remains highly uncertain. Tesla is currently a distant second in paid rides.
### Signal map
- 10 April 2026: Dutch RDW issued provisional EU type approval for FSD Supervised (eleport.com)
- 21 May 2026: Tesla launched FSD Supervised in China at 64,000 CNY (globalchinaev.com)
- March 2026: Waymo reached 500,000 paid weekly rides (techcrunch.com)
- July 2026: Tesla Robotaxi was active in 7 U.S. metros, with 2.5 million paid miles (businessinsider.com)

deepDive: ### Why the market values it

The allocation assumes a future manufacturing and services business that can replace human labor. The current price requires Tesla to reach volume production at costs that support positive contribution margins well within five years.
### Market structure and demand

Market estimates range from USD 15 billion to USD 29–48 billion by the early 2030s. A 10 percent share of a USD 20 billion market would generate USD 2 billion of revenue, far below what the EV allocation implies.
### Competitive position and economic moat
- Tesla Optimus: Pilot production; ~$50k–100k mfg cost
- Figure AI: >10,000 warehouse deployments; 1/hr production
- UBTECH / Unitree: Volume production (China); <$100k cost
### Unit economics and required scale

At a USD 30,000 ASP and 30 percent contribution margin, roughly 3 million units of annual volume would generate USD 27 billion of contribution. This remains below the EBIT needed to support the EV allocation.
### Economics bridge and gap
There is currently zero external revenue. Tesla would need to scale rapidly to hundreds of thousands of units at a sub-USD 40,000 ASP. The cost curve must improve as external demand emerges.
### Milestones and evidence needed
- Next 12–24 months: first dedicated Optimus line SOP
- Disclosed unit cost and first paid external customer
- Fremont operating at hundreds of thousands of units
### Assessment
Speculative. The allocation values a manufacturing business that does not yet operate at commercial scale and is disconnected from current pilot volumes.
### Signal map
- January 2026: reports of >1,000 Optimus Gen-3 on Fremont line (ifactoryapp.com)
- July 2026: Giga Texas ground-breaking for dedicated robot facility (teslarati.com)
- July 2026: Figure AI reported >10,000 warehouse deployments (technology.org)

valuePools.name: Automotive – Core Manufacturing, Sales & Bundled Services
deepDive: ### Why the market values it
Automotive still generates most current profit and supports the valuation bridge. The allocation assumes that price cuts and BYD competition do not permanently impair the earnings base.
### Market structure and demand
Tesla EV deliveries fell 8.6 percent in 2025 to 1.64 million vehicles, the second consecutive annual decline. Deliveries then recovered 25 percent y/y in Q2 2026.
### Competitive position and economic moat

BYD shipped 2.26 million BEVs in 2025. Tesla's bundled Supercharging, insurance, and software services provide some protection, but are not separately disclosed to confirm core hardware margin resilience.
### Unit economics and gap

Group EBIT margin fell from 16.8 percent in 2022 to 4.6 percent in 2025. The weakest assumption in the financial bridge is that Automotive margins stabilize while Tesla funds extensive investment in the option segments.

valuePools.name: Energy Generation & Storage
deepDive: ### Why the market values it
Energy is profitable, margin-accretive, and growing faster than Automotive. The EV allocation assumes continued deployment growth and a recovery in margins toward the mid-20s.
### Market structure and demand

Tesla deployed 46.7 GWh in 2025 and captured approximately 10 percent of global integrator share, behind BYD's 13 percent. Realistic share gains are likely in the premium utility and commercial segment.
### Competitive position and economic moat
BYD leads on volume, but Tesla's moat rests on Autobidder software integration, its large installed base of Powerwalls, and its reputation for bankability.
### Unit economics and gap

The segment recorded a 29.8 percent gross margin in 2025. In Q2 2026, this fell to 20.4 percent because of a USD 240 million warranty charge. The decline shows the risk from Chinese cell costs and tariffs.

data.segmentFinancialsSource: Tesla, Inc. Annual Report on Form 10-K for the Fiscal Year Ended December 31, 2025, pp. 97
data.valueBreakdownInterpretation: Tesla's USD 1.30 trillion enterprise value is disconnected from the earnings of its current cash-generating segments. Nearly two-thirds of the valuation, or USD 856 billion, is assigned to Autonomy and Optimus. These unproven segments generate zero disclosed operating profit. Automotive and Energy must fund these ventures while supporting the valuation.

executiveMap: Tesla generated USD 94.8 billion of net sales and USD 17.1 billion of gross profit in FY2025A. Nearly all came from its two reported segments. Automotive supplied 86.5 percent of sales and 77.8 percent of gross profit. Energy provided the balance at a higher 29.8 percent gross margin. The two emerging option segments have no separately disclosed revenue or profit. Segment values have been normalized to the Financial Data enterprise value control total of USD 1,295.8 billion.

The EV allocation is far ahead of current economics. Autonomy/Robotaxi/FSD and Optimus account for two-thirds of EV, despite producing essentially no standalone earnings today. The businesses that generate cash receive the remaining 33.9 percent. Tesla has net cash, with forward 2026 net debt of –USD 12.5 billion. The EV-to-equity bridge therefore reflects a small residual of other senior claims, approximately USD 10.6 billion, rather than leverage. Market capitalization of USD 1,297.7 billion maps almost one-for-one to the operating-asset allocation.

The allocation uses a single-bank SOTP framework, scaled uniformly by 17.7 percent to match the control EV. Confidence is medium for the two cash-generating segments and low for the option segments. Within months, the same bank's notes shifted their weights by more than 100 percent. The current share price of USD 328.58 requires the option segments to generate tens of billions of dollars of high-margin revenue within three-to-five years.
coreAnalysis.analyticalAnchor: Autonomy accounts for 44.6 percent of EV and requires the closest scrutiny. It must generate tens of billions of dollars of high-margin revenue within three-to-five years.
crossPoolBridge: The forecast assumes modest Automotive volume recovery, continued Energy GWh growth, and a gradual rise in EBIT margin from 4.6 percent to 9.6 percent. Automotive and Energy support all near-term EBITDA and FCF. The two option segments make no material contribution until late in the forecast period.
The weakest part of the bridge is the assumption that Automotive margins stabilize while Tesla funds the Cybercab and Optimus ramps.
The forecast requires delivery growth to continue in 2026–27 and Energy margins to recover from the Q2 2026 warranty charge. Optionality is not in the forecast; it appears only in the EV allocation.
coreAnalysis.bridgeMechanics: The bridge depends on continued volume recovery and EBIT-margin expansion in the existing hardware businesses while Tesla funds significant option-segment ramp-ups.
valuationRealityCheck: On a 15× 2026E EBIT basis, current earnings support only about 8 percent of allocated EV. Even a generous 12× EBITDA basis supports just 11 percent.
The remaining 89 percent depends on future monetization of Autonomy and Optimus.
The most fragile assumptions are the timing of unsupervised regulatory approval, Cybercab and Optimus cost curves, and the size of the 2030 robotaxi and humanoid markets.
The valuation can hold if these options reach the required scale. Existing Automotive and Energy earnings cannot justify it.
scenarios: The scenarios differ mainly in the two option segments. Autonomy timing and Optimus cost reductions drive the largest valuation swing.
The downside case assumes continued Automotive volume and margin erosion, plus a multi-year regulatory delay.
The upside case requires unsupervised robotaxi operations in dozens of cities and Optimus reaching commercial production at target cost.
coreAnalysis.bottomLine: The central question is whether Automotive and Energy cash flows can fund Tesla until Autonomy and Optimus generate the tens of billions of high-margin revenue already reflected in enterprise value. Autonomy matters most. It carries 44.6 percent of EV despite the thinnest evidence base and the most demanding regulatory and unit-economics requirements. Valuation depends mainly on optionality, not current earnings or assets. Tesla's net-cash position makes the EV-to-equity bridge straightforward, so equity holders capture nearly all upside or downside from the option segments. Portfolio managers should focus on unsupervised regulatory progress and the first disclosed robotaxi and Optimus unit-economics figures.

scenarioValuation.keyConditions: The scenarios differ mainly in the execution timing of the two option segments. The downside case assumes continued Automotive margin erosion and a multi-year regulatory delay. The upside case assumes unsupervised robotaxi operations in dozens of cities and Optimus reaching commercial production at target cost. These scenarios are operating boundary cases, not probability-weighted target-price inputs. The code-verified 12-month target of USD 230.2 sits between Bear and Base (Bear USD 167.6, Base USD 328.4, Bull USD 501.8); its method weights are shown in the Target Price Bridge.

risks.prose:
The investment case would break if unsupervised operations face a multi-year delay while Automotive margins continue to compress. That combination would leave the option EV unsupported as the main profit engine shrinks. Regulatory fragmentation across countries, including China’s 2027 L3/L4 rules, is only partly priced.

Investors may also underestimate the capital and management capacity needed to ramp Cybercab and Optimus while defending Automotive share against BYD. The risks are linked: a robotaxi safety incident would also damage FSD licensing and Optimus credibility.

### 3. Valuation Method Rationale

Tesla is an optionality-heavy growth company for which an explicit SOTP is conceptually preferred, but no standalone forecast revenue or EBITDA is supplied for the Autonomy and Optimus pools; therefore, 2027e EV/EBITDA is used as the independently calculable primary method, supported by 2027e P/E. Tesla trades at 96.2x 2027e EBITDA versus an indicative 11.1x peer median based on only two usable peers and versus its 101.83x normalized historical EV/EBITDA average; its 2027e P/E is 128.9x against a 112.06x normalized historical average. The Core Analysis’ full EV allocation corresponds to approximately 96.2x 2027e group EBITDA, supporting a 65.0x–95.0x fair-value band, although the large option pools remain weakly supported by disclosed economics. A 70.0x EV/EBITDA multiple is selected in the lower half of that band because robotaxi activity has expanded to seven U.S. metros and FSD approvals have progressed from the Netherlands to Lithuania, but Waymo retains a scale lead while Tesla has not disclosed robotaxi unit economics or Optimus external revenue. The 85.0x P/E cross-check similarly discounts Tesla’s historical premium for execution risk in the option pools. The XY ROE/P/BV signal receives a 0% weight because it does not capture Tesla’s future-profitability and optionality valuation structure; the principal multiple risk is a delay in unsupervised autonomy scaling alongside further Automotive margin pressure.
